title: Bringing page transitions to the web
summary: Jake Archibald (Google I/O 2022) shows the early version of what became the browser's View Transitions API, building up a single-page video site from a hard 'click, pop' cut to a tailored transition. The browser snapshots the old state, lets you change the DOM, then animates old and new snapshots with plain CSS; tagging elements lets persistent chrome stay put, lets a thumbnail morph into a different element on the next page, and lets you vary the motion by screen size, reduced-motion preference and navigation direction. (API names in the talk were later renamed: createDocumentTransition -> document.startViewTransition, page-transition-tag -> view-transition-name.)

insights.insight: The goal of a page transition is orientation, not decoration: it shows which content came from where and the direction of travel. The web default is an instant swap ('click, pop'), which throws that context away.
insights.quote: It's clear which information is coming from where and the direction of travel.
insights.visual: The Material music-app reference he admires: a tapped album tile has expanded into the full player, the artwork stays continuous across both states.

insights.insight: How the API works, and a reusable mental model for any SPA transition: freeze a snapshot of the old state, update the DOM underneath, then lay an overlay of old-snapshot and live-new layers on top and animate them (default: old 1->0, new 0->1 crossfade). When the animation ends the overlay disappears and the real page is revealed. Both states only need to exist as images for the duration.
insights.visual: Diagram of the pseudo-element tree (transition-container > image-wrapper > outgoing-image / incoming-image) next to the list page and the detail page it is transitioning between.

insights.insight: A whole-page slide makes elements that exist on both screens (the header) slide out only to slide back in, which reads as noise. Give persistent elements their own transition name so they are captured separately: they stay still (or just crossfade) while only the content that actually changes moves.
insights.quote: Ideally, it wouldn't move at all
insights.visual: Mobile demo mid-transition: the list of thumbnails slides out to the left while the detail page slides in from the right, but the purple '<- HTTP 203' header bar stays fixed on top.

insights.insight: Tagged elements also animate their size and position from the old box to the new box. Capturing just the site title separately makes it glide sideways to make room for the back arrow, a small, satisfying shift that ties the two states together. Layers are flattened into siblings, so nesting and overflow:hidden no longer block an element from travelling.
insights.visual: The header title 'HTTP 203' has shifted right to sit next to the new back arrow while the content below is still mid-slide.

insights.insight: The same motion can be right on a phone and too much on a big screen: a full-page lateral slide on desktop feels over the top, even dizzying. Swap keyframes per breakpoint with ordinary media queries (e.g. full slide on mobile, small fade-and-slide on desktop). And respect prefers-reduced-motion: skip, or make the motion very subtle, since 'reduced' is not 'none'.
insights.quote: it prefers reduced motion, not prefers no motion
insights.visual: Code: the navigate function falls back to a plain DOM update when the API is missing OR matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') matches.

insights.insight: Shared-element morph between DIFFERENT elements: just before navigating, give the clicked thumbnail the same transition name as the big video embed on the next page. The browser treats the thumbnail as the 'before' state of the embed, so it grows from its grid cell into the player while crossfading. The tag is set inline only for that click and removed afterwards.
insights.visual: Desktop demo caught mid-morph: the 'Zombie Dom' thumbnail has grown out of the grid to a larger card over the still-visible thumbnail grid, on its way to becoming the main embed.

insights.insight: Direction must match the navigation: forward slides in from one side, back from the other, and a shared element shrinks back to where it came from. Put a temporary class on <html> (e.g. 'back-transition') and let the CSS pick keyframes from it; the Navigation API tells you whether a navigation is a back/forward traversal.
insights.visual: Going back on desktop: the 'Gamepad API' detail card is shrinking back toward its thumbnail position while the grid fades back in behind it.

apply_to_wael: Build the first-launch flow on document.startViewTransition (with a no-op fallback): each step change (welcome -> level -> subject -> question -> result -> account) runs inside it, so React only swaps state and CSS on ::view-transition-old/new drives the motion.

Give the persistent layers their own view-transition-name so they never 'pop': the 3D island/town backdrop, Wael the character, and the top progress/XP bar. Only the step panel moves; Wael can glide to his new spot (size + position animate automatically) instead of being re-rendered.

Morph the chosen element into the next screen: give the tapped level chip or subject badge the same view-transition-name as the header badge of the next screen (set it on tap, clear after), so the badge flies up and becomes the game header.

Keep direction RTL-correct with a class on <html> (forward = new panel from the left, back = from the right), and add a prefers-reduced-motion branch that falls back to a short crossfade instead of slides and camera moves.
